title: Office Hours: Ask One Question
summary: Navigate asking for help despite fear of judgment. Practice preparing one clear question and choosing clarity over confidence.
author: HeyPsych Clinical Content Team
learningObjectives: Practice asking for help despite fear of looking stupid
Interpret neutral instructor responses as normal, not rejection
Close the loop with one actionable next step

nodes.text:
Your professor's office hours are in 15 minutes. You've been stuck on a concept from lecture and know you should ask—but your chest tightens at the thought.

'What if I sound stupid? What if I'm wasting their time? Everyone else probably gets it.'

What do you do?

You're standing outside the office. Through the half-open door, you hear another student asking questions. They sound confident, articulate. You compare yourself instantly: 'They know what they're doing. I'll just embarrass myself.'

The other student finishes and leaves, nodding politely as they pass you.

What do you do?

You open your laptop and draft an email instead. It feels safer—no eye contact, no real-time judgment, time to edit your words.

But as you type, you realize: the question is hard to explain over email. And waiting for a reply means staying stuck longer.

The professor replies: 'This is a great question—easier to explain in person. I have office hours tomorrow at 2pm if you want to stop by.'

You convince yourself you'll figure it out later. Maybe watch a YouTube video. Maybe ask a friend. Anything but going to office hours.

The relief is instant. But the concept stays confusing, and the assignment deadline creeps closer.

The night before it's due, you're still stuck.

You pull out your phone and type a quick note: 'I'm confused about [concept]. Can you explain how it connects to [example]?'

Having the question written down feels grounding. You take a breath.

You knock lightly and step inside.

The professor looks up. 'Hi, come in. What can I help you with?'

What do you say?

You step inside without a plan. The professor looks up.

'Hi, come in. What can I help you with?'

Your mind blanks. You know you're confused, but the words won't come together clearly.

What do you say?

You ask your question. The professor listens, nods, and responds:

'Good question. A lot of students find this tricky. Let me explain...'

They walk you through it. Their tone is neutral—not warm, not cold. Just... normal. Professional.

Your anxiety whispers: 'Are they annoyed? Did I waste their time?'

But their words say otherwise.

What do you do?

You start with: 'I'm really sorry to bother you, I know you're busy, but I'm just totally lost and probably should have figured this out already...'

The professor interrupts gently: 'It's okay. Office hours are for questions. What's confusing you?'

You manage to ask your question. The apologies came from a place of not wanting to be a burden—a feeling many people share.

They explain the concept. It helps, even if part of you still feels uncertain about whether you 'should have' asked.

You say: 'I just... don't really get the last lecture. It was confusing.'

The professor nods. 'Okay. What specifically was unclear?'

It's hard to pinpoint on the spot—putting confusion into words is genuinely difficult. They try to help, but without a specific question, the conversation feels scattered.

You leave wishing you had more clarity. That's okay—it's information for next time.

Before leaving, you ask: 'What's one thing I should focus on before the next class?'

The professor gives you a specific next step: 'Review [this example] and try [this practice problem]. That'll clarify it.'

You nod. You have a plan now.

You leave the office. The anxiety is still there, but quieter. You asked for help, you got an answer, and you have a clear next step.

Clarity beats confidence.

They finish explaining. You nod, say 'Thanks,' and head out.

As you walk away, you realize: you're not totally sure what to do next. You got an explanation, but not a concrete plan.

You showed up and asked—that's real progress. The next step is just getting clarity on what comes next.

Their tone was neutral. But your mind insists: 'They think I'm slow. They're annoyed. I shouldn't have come.'

You thank them quickly and leave. The explanation helped a little, but the mind-reading pulled you out of the moment.

You tried. But interpreting neutral as negative kept you from fully engaging.

choices.description: Preparing one clear question gives structure. You'll sound more confident because you're more prepared.
choices.resultText: You write it down. The question feels clearer now.

choices.resultText: You leave without closing the loop. Partial clarity.

choices.description: When we're anxious, neutral responses can feel negative. This is a common pattern worth noticing.
choices.resultText: You interpret neutrality as judgment. The anxiety spikes.

choices.description: The professor made it easy. They literally invited you. This is your second chance.

choices.description: The deadline pressure finally outweighs the anxiety. You reach out.
choices.resultText: You send a short email: 'Can I stop by office hours tomorrow? I'm stuck on the assignment.' They reply: 'Of course. See you then.'

choices.text: Leave with a clear next step

You showed up, but didn't fully commit. Progress, but incomplete.
Avoidance won. The confusion stays, and the pattern continues.

endings.title: Confident Step
endings.text:
You did the hard thing. You went to office hours, asked a clear question, and—critically—closed the loop by asking for one next step.

Clarity beats confidence. You didn't need to feel perfectly sure of yourself. You just needed to show up, ask directly, and get specific.

This is what asking for help looks like when you do it well: uncomfortable, brief, effective.

Next time will still be hard. But you know the formula now.

endings.title: Mixed But Moving
endings.text:
You went. That's more than avoiding. You showed up, asked something, and got some help—even if you over-apologized, left without a next step, or let mind-reading pull you out of the moment.

You're building the skill. It's messy. That's normal.

Next time, try one thing: ask for a clear next step before you leave. Close the loop. That's the difference between partial help and real progress.

endings.title: Avoidance Loop
endings.text:
You chose safety over clarity. Maybe you emailed instead, or skipped entirely, or bailed at the door.

Avoidance feels like relief—until you're still stuck on the concept, still confused, still avoiding the next time.

Office hours aren't about confidence. They're about getting unstuck. And the only way to get unstuck is to ask.

Next time, try this: write down one clear question, walk to the door, and ask it. That's the whole rep.
